name: Lightning Process

card.summary: A trademarked three-day mind-body training course for chronic fatigue and other long-term symptoms, taken by people who hope restored energy will let them train, work and look like themselves again.
card.note: NICE advised in 2021 against offering it to people with ME/CFS; some participants report worsening or feeling blamed.

quick.overview:
The Lightning Process is a three-day group training programme created by British osteopath and NLP practitioner Phil Parker. It teaches participants to notice and interrupt what the programme describes as a persistent stress response. It is used mainly for ME/CFS and, more recently, long COVID.

Its link to appearance is indirect: people who report recovering energy describe being able to exercise, sleep, attend school or work and look after themselves again, which in turn affects physique, skin and general presentation. A randomised trial in adolescents and several smaller studies exist, and national guidance on ME/CFS has taken a different view of the approach.
quick.how: Participants attend three consecutive days of group sessions (about 12 hours in total) led by a trained practitioner. The sessions combine coaching, postural awareness and movement with a stepwise mental routine that participants practise until it becomes habitual. Proponents describe the aim as retraining the nervous system's stress response.
quick.risks: Some participants report worsening of symptoms after the course, and critics describe people feeling blamed when they did not improve. In 2021 NICE advised against offering the Lightning Process to people with ME/CFS, and the UK Advertising Standards Authority upheld complaints about ME/CFS claims on the programme's website in 2012. It is not a substitute for medical assessment of persistent fatigue.

lead: The Lightning Process (LP) is a trademarked three-day personal training programme developed in the late 1990s by Phil Parker, a British osteopath and neuro-linguistic programming practitioner. It is delivered to groups by trained practitioners and teaches participants to recognise what the programme describes as an acute stress response and to interrupt it using a learned sequence of steps, drawing on osteopathy, life coaching and NLP [1][2][3].

Its connection to looks is a chain rather than a direct effect. People who take the course are typically living with chronic fatigue, and those who report improvement describe regaining the energy to exercise, keep regular sleep, attend school or work, eat and groom as they did before illness. Training consistency, sleep and activity are the everyday inputs to physique, skin and overall presentation, which is how the programme is relevant to someone trying to improve how they look [4].

Research includes a pilot and a pragmatic randomised trial in adolescents with mild or moderate CFS/ME, a 2021 systematic review of existing studies, qualitative studies, and small case series in cancer survivors and long COVID [4][5][8][9][10][11]. UK guidance and regulators have taken a more cautious position [2].

chain: Three-day mind-body course aimed at a persistent stress response
Reported improvement in fatigue and daily function
More exercise, school or work and self-care
Better physique, sleep and general appearance
angle.text: People use the Lightning Process to tackle chronic fatigue that keeps them from training and daily routines. Participants who improve describe having the energy to return to the habits that shape how they look, such as exercise, regular sleep and grooming.

paras: The programme runs over three consecutive days of group sessions, around 12 hours in total, led by a practitioner trained and licensed by the programme's creator [1][2]. According to the SMILE trial protocol, it is derived from osteopathy, life-coaching and neuro-linguistic programming [3].

Practitioners teach participants to recognise what they describe as the body's acute stress response and to calm it, using posture, movement and personal coaching, followed by a stepwise routine that is rehearsed until it becomes habitual. The stated rationale is that a persistent stress response, perhaps set off by infection, psychological stress or trauma, can be maintained by the nervous system and then released by conscious practice [1].

Phil Parker developed the programme in the late 1990s and trademarked it [1]. In the early 2010s researchers estimated that more than 250 children with CFS/ME in the UK attended courses each year, which prompted the first trial work [3][5].

Uptake has extended beyond CFS/ME. Parker has described benefits for conditions including depression, panic attacks, insomnia and chronic pain, and practitioners and clinicians have since applied it to long COVID and fatigue in cancer survivors [1][10][11].

Proponents say that fatigue and other symptoms can be maintained by a conditioned stress response and that participants can learn to switch it off. Participants in qualitative studies describe the course as a turning point and report feeling more in control of their symptoms [7]. Small surveys and case series report high rates of self-assessed recovery [11][12].

A feasibility randomised trial in 56 children aged 12 to 18 at a specialist NHS paediatric service found recruitment, randomisation and both treatment arms feasible and acceptable [5]. The full SMILE trial randomised 100 adolescents with mild to moderate CFS/ME to specialist medical care alone or with the Lightning Process added. At six months, physical function scores were higher in the group that received the programme (adjusted difference 12.5 points), and the difference was larger at 12 months; fatigue and anxiety were also lower at 6 months, with depression and school attendance improved by 12 months [4]. The trial was open-label, so participants knew which arm they were in [4].

A 2021 systematic review of 14 studies of the programme noted variation in quality, with earlier studies lacking control groups, and identified an emerging evidence base that includes the randomised trial [8]. Reviews of paediatric CFS/ME treatment have cited the SMILE result while noting that the evidence base overall is small and affected by differing diagnostic criteria [6][9]. A mixed-methods pilot examined the programme for fatigue in adolescent and young adult cancer survivors, and a case report and a 12-patient audit described its use in long COVID, with all 12 audit participants reporting no harm from the intervention [10][11][13].

In 2011 Hampshire Trading Standards referred the programme's website to the UK Advertising Standards Authority, which upheld two of four complaints, finding that claims about ME/CFS were misleading because the supporting studies lacked controls; the website was amended [14]. In October 2021 NICE's ME/CFS guideline advised against offering the Lightning Process, or therapies based on it [14]. In August 2022 the World ME Alliance said it did not endorse the programme [14].

Commentators have criticised reliance on self-reported outcomes that reflect what the course teaches, and the programme's ownership of improvement while attributing non-response to the participant [14]. A 2024 BBC File on 4 report included an account of a coach telling a reporter that symptoms were maintained by her thoughts, and a neuroscientist who said the programme borrows neuroscience terminology [14].

Some patients report deterioration after the course, and critics say patients can come away feeling responsible when the approach does not help; a BMJ report described children who felt blamed when they did not improve [14]. A Norwegian report in a medical journal described patient experiences with the course [12]. The 12-case long COVID audit and the SMILE publications reported no harms from the programme in those samples [4][13].

The programme is not a looks-focused product and sits at the edge of appearance communities. It surfaces mainly where people discuss restoring energy and capacity after long illness, with the stated payoff being a return to training and normal routines.

timeline.event: Phil Parker develops the Lightning Process [14].
Feasibility trial recruits 56 children at an NHS paediatric CFS/ME service [5].
Hampshire Trading Standards refers the programme's website to the ASA; ruling published 2012 [14].
SMILE randomised trial results published in Archives of Disease in Childhood [4].
Systematic review of the evidence base published; NICE advises against offering the programme for ME/CFS [8][14].
Case report on long COVID published; BBC File on 4 episode on the programme [11][14].
